The minimal toy: one rigid flat-foldable vertex with sector angles 60°, 90°, 120° and 90°, whose configuration space is two folding modes meeting only at the flat state, and a declared resource, the plan area of the smallest convex tray that holds it. Folded states cost 0.75 and 0.875; every switch between them passes the flat state, which costs 1 + √3/2 ≈ 1.866, so the bottleneck budget is 1.866 and the reconfiguration slack 0.991. At a budget of 1.5 the sublevel set cuts each branch near flat and both states are held but neither reaches the other. Its form follows Foschi, Hull and Ku's equations as read in NOTE-1606, with coefficients the filer computed and checked and the two-mode structure derived in the case; it also draws on Abel et al. | [CASE-207](../../../record/cases.d/CASE-207.md) v2 | The square twist | Filed at the owner's request on 2026-11-05, to file "one or more CASEs for origami as a toy model of a resource bounded constraint configuration space". Silverberg et al. 2015 ([NOTE-1554](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1554.md)): the square twist's crease pattern is isostatic, and rigidly it has only two isolated states, unfolded and folded, yet it folds by bending its facets, a hidden degree of freedom with its own energy scale. The authors' thesis is that the number of degrees of freedom changes with the energy scale probed; their kinematic skeleton, with bending capped at 10°, has a critical plane angle near 23° separating a connected configuration space from a disconnected one. K linear operators, identical in form and differing only by initialization, mix by context-conditioned shares. Four rules update the shares: ordinary mixture-of-experts gating (the baseline), the same gating with a load-balancing loss, the same gating with a usage bias, and a multiplicative rule driven by the collective's loss minus the operator's own. Training follows influence. Each rule was run with K = 4 (no spare operator) and K = 6 (two spare), in 6 seeds, followed by eleven test arms. Every rule differentiated, with a distinct specialist for the rare context in 6 of 6 seeds. With K = 4, participation and performance matched across three rules. A rare specialist made rare (share 10⁻³, frozen) recovered in 6 of 6 seeds under all four rules. Under the multiplicative rule its growth rate did not depend on how rare it was made. Under gradient gating it fell with the share, and from 10⁻⁵ the specialist did not recover within the window. A usage bias recovered it from any share, but also raised an incompetent copy to 0.19. With K = 6, a removed specialist was replaced by a spare in 6 of 6 seeds under every rule. A suppressed specialist then failed to return in 23 of 24 rule-seed pairs per arm, whether its training had been decoupled from its influence and whether it had kept its competence. With K = 4, nothing replaced a removed specialist. A suppressed one returned every time, even after weight decay had cost it most of its competence and with its parameters frozen. [CASE-099](../../../record/cases.d/CASE-099.md)'s meaning–authority loop is built as a bounded simulation inside one mind. Authority sets attention and so attenuates readings against it, and it is scored against the dominant interpretation. The world switches every 300 steps, and nothing the loop does changes the world or when inputs arrive. With sensory input alone the loop locks in on every seed. Removing an evidence channel (the senses, the body, testimony) leaves it blind, unless capture goes with it. Fixed-weight DeGroot and Friedkin–Johnsen, and the reflected-appraisal power maps of DeGroot–Friedkin and Friedkin 2011, cannot make the winner of authority depend on the initial interpretation, and none of them, nor Gaussian bounded confidence, lets corpus imbalance switch authority with hysteresis; the reduced model does both. | [CASE-406](../../../record/cases.d/CASE-406.md) | Equal-budget interventions at different places | [CLAIM-562](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-562.md) holds, from mechanical systems, that where an intervention acts in a constraint structure can predict success better than how much intervention there is. A search of open evaluations for its organizational test, coded under six criteria fixed before the search, found one case that meets the standard: in Andhra Pradesh's randomized evaluation of 500 government primary schools, an individual teacher bonus, an extra contract teacher and a block grant for materials each cost about Rs 10,000 per school a year, and the bonus raised test scores by 0.27 SD against 0.09 SD for the two inputs. Place there is confounded with conditionality. Two cases come closest: Seva Mandir's immunisation camps, where the demand-side incentive was only ever added to the supply-side camps, and Zambia's supply chain pilot, two arms at two tiers whose costs are in a paper not reached. No case tests whether adding an intervention can make an organization fail. The wording is the assistant's (Claude, in this session); adopting it is the owner's call. | Proposed |
| [CASE-415](../../../record/cases.d/CASE-415.md) v2 | Four governance architectures, federated | [LEAD-180](../../../record/leads.d/LEAD-180.md) asked for [CASE-108](../../../record/cases.d/CASE-108.md) to be run. A small federated learner (scratch/studies/lead-180/) has a main block of tasks every specialist's data covers and a minority block only 3 honest dissenters' data covers; the 14 cooperatives misjudge it, and 3 adversaries farm for 100 rounds, then attack the main block (overt) or the minority block (mimic, looking like dissent). Unrestricted, two reliability-weighted, role-limited and adaptive aggregation, and an oracle, over 30 seeds. Role-limited audit, in which evaluators with their own validation evidence vote only on the blocks they hold evidence for, cut attack success to about 0 for both attacks and raised minority capability from 0.27 to 0.92, for 0.01 of main capability and 120 evaluations a round. Reputation by agreement was captured by the mimic attack (attack success 0.39, unrestricted 0.30); reputation by validation without jurisdiction stopped the overt attack and left the minority where unrestricted aggregation leaves it. With 2 of 7 evaluators compromised, role-limited audit let the mimic attack through (0.27) and cut the dissenters' influence from 4.2 to 0.9 times parity; the adaptive arm held it to 0.10 with an honest monitor and did no better than role-limited with a compromised one, which suspended every dissenter. With no evidence on the minority block independent of the proposals, attack success in a world and in its relabelling (dissenters' and attackers' targets swapped) summed to 1 for every architecture. Much follows from the stated rules. The wording is the assistant's (Claude, in this session); adopting it is the owner's call. | Active |
| [CASE-420](../../../record/cases.d/CASE-420.md) v2 | Role-indexed vs scalar grants | The study [LEAD-190](../../../record/leads.d/LEAD-190.md) asks for. Twenty operators, half on each side, each a reader with a meaning and a specialist retrieving for the others, as in [CASE-363](../../../record/cases.d/CASE-363.md)'s model, which is loaded unchanged. Critic weights (whose evidence one reads) are scored by agreement, by observed relevance, or a mix; decision grants set authority under one-hop, leave-one-out or recursive aggregation, and operators move them for realized policy or for authority held. Five grant schemes and six grant games, on 30 populations, in mean field and at agent level. Role indexing with the critic role scored by relevance leaves no factions and no capture; scalar grants fail either way; operators bound by both conditions delegate everything, all of it to their own side, beyond one hop too, and within their side to its extremes. A fictional model, by construction; the numbers are of this model. The wording is the assistant's (Claude, in this session); adopting it is the owner's call. | Active |
